source.title: Select, Hypothesize and Verify: Towards Verified Neuron Concept Interpretation
source.authors: Ze-Bin Ji; Yang Hu; Xiu-Li Bi; Bo Liu; Bin Xiao

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including references, is present.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates whether neuron concepts predict activation on generated inputs, using a visual-neuron method and Activation Rate rather than the language-model setting in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports Activation Rate outcomes for neuron-concept methods, including comparisons, ablations, threshold settings, and domain shift. These results bear on V6's question of whether concepts inferred from activating examples also predict activation on new inputs. It does not test the share of poles with one or two jobs, language-model neurons, attribution graphs, or explanations scored on new text. CLIP and MPNet similarity scores are omitted because they do not measure activation prediction. Table 4's AR results are included, but its flattened checkmark layout does not reliably identify each component configuration.
record.test_reason: The study infers concepts from a neuron's top-activating images, then generates new images of each concept and measures how often they push the neuron above its top-1% threshold (Activation Rate). For standard explanation methods (Network Dissection, MILAN, FALCON, DnD, CLIP-Dissect, WWW), this directly tests V6: whether explanations fitted to activating examples predict where the neuron fires on new inputs. The setting is vision penultimate-layer neurons with generated images, not language-model neurons with new text.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors argue that existing methods wrongly assume every neuron has a well-defined function and every generated concept is accurate. SIEVE filters low-discrimination neurons and verifies concepts on generated images. They report retained concepts activating neurons about 1.5x as often as the prior best method. That gain partly reflects SIEVE discarding hypotheses below the mean AR.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes penultimate-layer neurons in vision classifiers and tests concept hypotheses on generated images using Activation Rate; it does not reproduce a language-model neuron explanation audit.
record.method_sensitivity: Domain shift lowers Activation Rate for all methods; the paper reports β values from 4 to 12 with minimal change in the metrics.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating ResNet-50 neuron 39 (cat eyes) mainly lowers accuracy on feline classes (figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual vision-model neurons can have class-specific causal effects consistent with their concept.

fits_no_version.finding: A verification-based tool that discards low-AR hypotheses and low-discrimination neurons yields retained concepts with about 85% mean AR, versus about 50–58% for prior tools.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Testing explanations on generated inputs and filtering raises the predictive accuracy of the kept neuron explanations. This is not the same as a rise in the share of interpretable neurons (V4), because neurons and hypotheses are discarded.

record.problems: The paper reports aggregate mean Activation Rates rather than per-neuron failure proportions. It tests vision models with generated images, not language models with new text. It gives no uncertainty estimates for the reported metrics. Table 4's flattened component checkmarks make the row-to-configuration mapping unclear.
record.rows_left_out: No additional Activation Rate results omitted. CLIP cosine and MPNet cosine table values were left out because they do not measure activation prediction. Table 4's five mean-AR values are retained as R27–R31, with their component configurations marked unrecoverable from the flattened table.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B neuron pole shares (one job, two jobs, not understood).
Language models, dense and mixture-of-experts, scale to trillions of parameters.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose, recursive generalization.
Causes of messy neurons (architecture, regularization) and shares of interpretable neurons in InceptionV1-sized models.
Neuron-based attribution graphs versus replacement models.
Language-model neurons and explanations tested on new text; per-neuron failure proportions (only means are reported); recall-type prediction (whether the neuron fires where the concept is absent).
Simulation-based scoring of explanations on new text and the share of well-scored neurons.

missing.what: Per-neuron example: two concepts inferred from the same high-activation images get AR 0.26 (small round beards/whiskers) vs 0.98 (curly dense coat), showing an activating-example-consistent explanation that fails to predict firing.
Fraction of neurons or hypotheses removed by the Select threshold β and by the Verify mean-AR filter. The paper does not report it, so the share of neurons with a verified concept is unknown.

record.verdict_notes: Chance under the top-1% threshold is about 1%, so baseline ARs of about 50% are far above chance yet well short of full prediction. That fits V6's 'explains less than inspection suggests' rather than 'explains nothing'. It is unclear whether the mean-AR filter was applied to the baseline methods. The text describes it as part of SIEVE's Verify step, so baseline rows were treated as unfiltered. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The study is vision-only, so it bears on V6's general claim, not the language-model audit setting. The tranche could arguably be T3 (new setting); T2 is kept because the measure targets the same question.

versions.untested_parts: The proportion of Qwen3-32B neuron poles with one, two, or not-yet-understood jobs.
Language models, dense or mixture-of-experts models, and scale up to trillions of parameters.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, and recursive generalization.
Architecture or regularization as causes of messy neurons, and interpretable-neuron shares in InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons and whether they explain behavior without a replacement model.
The paper tests visual-neuron concepts against generated images, not language-model explanations against new text; it does not report per-neuron failure rates.
Scoring explanations by simulated activations on new text, and the proportion of language-model neurons receiving good scores.

relation.reason: The study's own measurements of the baseline explanation methods bear directly on V6.

tranche.reason: It uses a different method (images generated from each concept, scored by Activation Rate over the top-1% threshold) on the same question: whether explanations taken from activating examples predict firing.

source_check.notes: R40/R41 repeat Table 3 values (R22/R24) under the wrong subject; drop them or relink them to the Places365 ResNet-18. AR has no random or control-concept baseline. SIEVE's own 75-86% comes after discarding hypotheses below the initial mean AR, so its comparison with the baselines is not like-for-like. The text names no venue (arXiv v1, cs.CV).

statements.correction: 2603.24953: arXiv preprint (cs.CV), no venue stated, no code, no controls. Its models are ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 on ImageNet-1K, ResNet-18 on Places365, and a ResNet-18 trained on remote-sensing data (Eurosat, Table 6).
statements.problem: The numbers for this study are right: baseline range 45.01-58.32, ResNet-50 ND 45.01, CLIP-Dissect 55.16/57.91, Eurosat 43.16/37.43. But the 'why' line calls the study 'CVPR'. The text is the arXiv v1 preprint [cs.CV] and names no venue, so 'Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition' is the arXiv category, not the conference. Also, the conditions line says 'trained on ImageNet or Places365', yet the 'what' also cites the remote-sensing (Eurosat) ResNet-18.
Minor: Network Dissect (45.01) uses Broden as both probe and concept set, while CLIP-Dissect (57.91) uses ImageNet val with Common Words. The probe set changes along with the method.

reader_labels.condition: Visual neuron-concept methods and tested datasets
reader_labels.reason: Mean Activation Rates are below 100% for the reported methods, indicating that generated images matching inferred concepts do not always produce significant neuron activation; the study reports this across the comparisons and settings in R1–R42.
